To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Laurentide and Cordillera ice sheets in northeastern British Columbia were confluent between 59°N and 60°N.

(1) ice sheet margins were located between 59°N and 60°N at the onset of deglaciatiion, (2) ice sheets retreated into uplands and the Liard plateau, (3) meltwater and sediment transport continued until the end of glacial conditions, (4) glacial lakes were sustained by remnant glaciers and ice in the Liardi and Fort Nelson river drainage basins, and (5) glacial lake drainage occurred through incised spillways.
the pattern and style (including the rate of retreat and meltwater drainage) of deglaciation in the study area is complex, but the timing is constrained by optical ages.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the pattern and style by which Late Wisconsinan ice sheets retreated and the timing of glacial lake formation and drainage at the northern confluences of the Cordilleran and Laurentide ice sheets in northwestern Canada.
the pattern and style (timing, rate, and direction of ice sheet retreat and glacial lake drainage) of deglaciation in northeastern British Columbia and adjacent Yukon Territory.

the pattern and style (i.e., timing, rates, directions, and processes) of Late Wisconsinan deglaciation in the northern Rockies of British Columbia and southern Mackenzie Mountain foothills of the Northwest Territories.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the pattern of deglaciation in northeastern British Columbia is characterized by a complex interaction of the Laurentide and Cordillera ice sheets, and by the formation and drainage of glacial lakes Peace, Hay, Liard, and Fort Nelson.
the pattern of deglaciation was controlled by the configuration and retreat of ice sheets, with meltwater drainage and lake formation occurring as the ice retreated.
the Laurentide ice sheet retreated from northeastern British Columbia in two stages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ice-sheet deglaciation was rapid, and that the pattern and style was controlled by the presence of a large ice mass, the Liard Plateaus, and a high-elevation mountain barrier.

the Laurentide ice sheet retreated northeastward from the terminal limit in the Peace River valley to the Liard Plateua and Mackenzie Mountains by 12.8 ± 1.0 ka, with the last ice retreat from the Liard Plateu to the Mackenzie Mountains by ca. 11.8 ka.
the Cordilleran ice margin was not as far north as was previously thought and that the Laurentide ice margin in north-central British Columbia was farther south than has been suggested.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pattern and style for the retreat of the Cordilleran and Laurentide ice sheets were different in this area.
the pattern and style for deglaciation in this part of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet was different than the pattern and style at the southern margin of the ice sheet in the Rocky Mountains.
ice sheet retreat was more complex than previously thought.
